blogs.title: Four small signs of fragrant cardamom
blogs.excerpt: A simple guide to looking, smelling and storing cardamom so its character stays part of the meal.
blogs.imageAlt: Green cardamom pods with aromatic whole spices

sections.heading: Start with the pod
paragraphs: Choose pods that feel intact and substantial for their size. Natural variation in colour is normal; freshness is better judged by the pod's aroma and condition than by a single shade of green.
If the pods are badly crushed or very dry, some of their aroma may already have escaped.

sections.heading: Let the aroma tell you more
paragraphs: Crush one pod gently between your fingers. A good pod should open with a lively, sweet, citrus-like fragrance. A faint or flat smell can be a sign that it has been stored for a long time or left exposed to air.

sections.heading: Keep it whole until you need it
paragraphs: Whole pods protect their seeds from air and light. Store them in a tightly closed container in a cool, dry cupboard, then crack or grind only the amount you plan to use.

sections.heading: A little goes a long way
paragraphs: Cardamom can be gently fragrant or boldly aromatic depending on how much you use. Start small, taste, and add more if the dish needs it.

blogs.title: Whole or ground? How to use cardamom in the kitchen
blogs.excerpt: Choose the right form for chai, a slow-cooked curry, a delicate dessert or a quick weekday bake.
blogs.imageAlt: A spiced tea served in a cup

sections.heading: Whole pods for a slow infusion
paragraphs: Use whole, lightly cracked pods when you want cardamom to perfume a liquid over time. They work beautifully in chai, rice, custards and slow-simmered sauces, and can be removed before serving.

sections.heading: Ground seeds for an even finish
paragraphs: Freshly ground seeds blend smoothly into cake batter, cookie dough and spice mixes. Grind only what you need so the aroma does not fade while it waits in the jar.

sections.heading: Match the form to the dish
paragraphs: A whole pod gives a gentle, gradual note. Ground cardamom reaches every bite and tastes more immediate. When a recipe is flexible, begin with a small amount and adjust to taste.

blogs.title: The everyday rituals that begin with elaichi
blogs.excerpt: A crushed pod in morning tea, a pinch in payasam: cardamom makes ordinary pauses feel considered.
blogs.imageAlt: A warm cup of Indian chai with spices

sections.heading: A familiar cup, made your own
paragraphs: In many homes, cardamom is part of the tea tin and the morning routine. A pod or two can make the kitchen smell welcoming before the first cup reaches the table.

sections.heading: The finishing touch in sweets
paragraphs: A small pinch of ground elaichi can lift rice pudding, milk sweets and festive bakes. Add it near the end of cooking so its delicate fragrance stays present.

sections.heading: Share the moment
paragraphs: The best rituals are rarely complicated. Brew an extra cup, set out a small plate of something sweet and let the conversation take its time.

blogs.title: Cardamom belongs in savoury cooking, too
blogs.excerpt: From fragrant rice to a slow-cooked stew, whole pods add a floral, warm note beyond dessert.
blogs.imageAlt: Biryani rice layered with herbs and spices

sections.heading: Let the whole spice bloom
paragraphs: Add lightly bruised pods to warm oil or ghee with other whole spices. A short, gentle sizzle helps release their fragrance before the rice, vegetables or broth go in.

sections.heading: Keep the balance
paragraphs: Cardamom is distinctive, so pair it with intention. Cinnamon, cloves, cumin and black pepper make familiar companions, but the right balance depends on the dish.

sections.heading: Finish with freshness
paragraphs: For a brighter note, crush a seed or two and stir them in just before serving. The aroma will meet the steam as the dish reaches the table.
